title: The greater array (Sn 4.13)
hookLine: read it: the sage doesn't join the argument
tomorrow: and if you want that peace, how fast can it come?

lines: NOT VOTING FEELS LIKE A VOTE.
cards: Somebody in the group chat posts a poll, and suddenly not voting feels like a vote. The next poem in the chapter of eights, the Greater Array, answers yesterday's question, but it starts with a strange detail.
The questioner asks: these people who say only this is true, do they only get blame, or praise too? You'd expect the poem to say the winner gets the prize. Instead it says praise is a small thing.
Too small, it says, to bring peace. Why would the prize be too small?

teach.h: PRAISE IS TOO SMALL FOR PEACE.
teach.b: The Greater Array, Sutta Nipata 4.13, says an argument bears two fruits: praise and blame. Win and you get praise. Lose and you get blame.
Both grow on the same tree, and you can't pick one without planting the other. So even the good fruit doesn't buy peace; it just keeps you on the battlefield, waiting for the next round.
Seeing this, the poem says, don't dispute, and see the place where there's no dispute as the safe one. Then it watches the arguers more closely.
People live inside their views like houses. Some say purity comes from what they've seen, or heard, or from rules and vows kept just so. Each calls his own teaching complete and the other's poor.

The poem's reply: if a teaching became poor just because a rival called it that, none would be worth anything, since everyone says it about everyone. And where does the wise one stand? Not in a house of views.
The sage, the poem says, doesn't take sides when disputes arise. Peaceful among those who aren't, unmoved while others grab. Notice what that is not.
It isn't silence, and it isn't not caring; the Buddha is answering a question as he says it.
It's not joining: speaking without moving into a camp.

how: Theravada teachers often read the chapter of eights' poems on views together and use them to talk about speech: saying what one sees without turning a conversation into a contest.

o: a poem on why the wise one won't take sides in disputes
a battle plan from an old story about rival kings
a long list of the rules for settling a quarrel

games.q: the greater array — tap the pairs.
p: takes no side when disputes arise

s: not joining means staying silent and not caring how things turn out
the Buddha answers the question as he teaches it. the sage speaks; he just doesn't move into a camp.
the poem says even winning an argument brings too little to give peace
win and you get praise, and praise is a small thing, not enough for peace.

games.q: at a family dinner, two cousins start in on a hot topic and turn to you: whose side are you on? what does the greater array point toward?
o: say what you honestly see, without taking a side in the contest.
back the cousin with the better argument, so the fight ends sooner.
leave the table; staying out means not being part of it at all.
games.why: the sage in the poem doesn't take sides when disputes arise, yet the Buddha is speaking the whole time. not joining is staying at the table without moving into a camp.

practice: Sit with your hands resting open on your knees, palms up, jaw soft. When a thought arrives that wants to argue, a reply, a comeback, a correction, notice it in the hands first: do they want to close?
Let them stay open, and let the thought pass by without picking it up.

wordCard.voice: The Greater Array: Sutta Nipata 4.13, the longer twin of yesterday's poem, named for the same lines drawn up for battle. Arguments bear praise and blame, and praise is too small for peace.

orig.note: Pali: dispute, quarrel. The poem's safe place is where there is no vivada.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: not joining, which is different from not caring. Day sixteen sixty-eight, done.

sources.ref: Sutta Nipata 4.13 (Mahaviyuha Sutta, the Greater Array)
